subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Planning Fallacy
description: A 60-second lesson on The Planning Fallacy.

hook.text: The Sydney Opera House was budgeted for 4 years and $7 million. It took 16 years and $102 million.

buildup.text: We consistently underestimate time, cost, and risk while overestimating our own efficiency.

discovery.text: The planning fallacy: we plan based on best-case scenarios and ignore what happened in similar past cases.

twist.text: People who've experienced delays on past projects still underestimate the next one. Memory doesn't fix it.

climax.text: The fix: check how long similar projects actually took. Use history, not hope, as your baseline.

punchline.text: Plans are wishes. History is data.

quiz.question: What causes the planning fallacy?
options: Basing plans on best-case scenarios and ignoring history
Having too much data to process

details.summary: The planning fallacy is the systematic tendency to create overly optimistic estimates by focusing on the specific details of a plan rather than consulting the base rate of similar past projects. People use the inside view of their unique plan instead of the outside view of comparable outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: Budget overruns, deadline failures, and project cancellations are direct consequences of the planning fallacy. From kitchen renovations to Olympic stadiums, initial estimates are almost always too optimistic because planners imagine the specific.
takeaways: People plan for best-case scenarios rather than typical outcomes
The inside view focuses on unique details while the outside view consults base rates
Reference class forecasting systematically corrects for the planning fallacy

faq.question: Why do experienced planners still fall for the planning fallacy?
faq.answer: Because each new project feels unique, experienced planners use the inside view: imagining this specific project going smoothly. They do not consult the base rate of their own past projects, most of which also felt unique yet still overran their estimates.

faq.question: What is reference class forecasting and how does it help?
faq.answer: Reference class forecasting starts by identifying similar past projects and using their actual outcomes as the starting estimate, then adjusting for specific factors. By starting from outside-view base rates rather than inside-view optimism, estimates become dramatically more accurate.
